There’s no single universal ranking—“top” depends on whether you mean **strategy prestige, implementation scale, industry specialization, or employer reputation**. A practical shortlist is:

### Top-tier strategy firms — “MBB”
These are generally regarded as the most prestigious global strategy consultancies:

1. **McKinsey & Company** — corporate strategy, transformation, operations, public sector  
2. **Boston Consulting Group (BCG)** — strategy, innovation, growth, digital and advanced analytics  
3. **Bain & Company** — private equity, corporate strategy, performance improvement, customer strategy  

Together, these are commonly called **MBB**. In Vault’s 2026 North America employer ranking, Bain ranked first and BCG second; McKinsey remains one of the most prominent global strategy firms. ([legacy.vault.com](https://legacy.vault.com/best-companies-to-work-for/consulting/vault-consulting-rankings-top-50?utm_source=openai))

### Other highly regarded strategy firms

- **Oliver Wyman**
- **Kearney**
- **L.E.K. Consulting**
- **Roland Berger**
- **Arthur D. Little**
- **OC&C Strategy Consultants**
- **Monitor Deloitte**
- **EY-Parthenon**
- **Strategy&** — PwC’s strategy practice

These firms are especially strong in areas such as financial services, private equity, healthcare, consumer goods, industrials, transportation, and restructuring.

### Large-scale transformation and technology consulting

- **Accenture**
- **Deloitte**
- **PwC**
- **EY**
- **KPMG**
- **IBM Consulting**
- **Capgemini**

These firms typically offer broader implementation, technology, systems integration, risk, and operational transformation capabilities in addition to strategy. Consultancy.org’s global management-consulting listings include many of these firms among the leading providers, though rankings vary significantly by methodology. ([consultancy.org](https://www.consultancy.org/rankings/top-consulting-firms-by-area-of-expertise/management?utm_source=openai))

### Strong specialist and boutique firms

- **Alvarez & Marsal** — restructuring, performance improvement, disputes  
- **FTI Consulting** — economic consulting, disputes, restructuring, investigations  
- **Korn Ferry** — leadership, organization, talent  
- **PA Consulting** — innovation, public sector, technology  
- **Analysis Group** — economics, healthcare, litigation  
- **Cornerstone Research** — economic and financial analysis  
- **The Bridgespan Group** — nonprofit and social-impact strategy  
- **ghSMART** — executive assessment and leadership advisory  

### Quick rule of thumb

- **Most prestigious general strategy brand:** McKinsey, BCG, Bain  
- **Best for implementation and technology:** Accenture, Deloitte  
- **Best for private equity:** Bain, L.E.K., McKinsey, BCG, EY-Parthenon  
- **Best for restructuring:** Alvarez & Marsal, FTI, AlixPartners  
- **Best for economic/litigation consulting:** Analysis Group, Cornerstone, Charles River Associates, Brattle  
- **Best for organization and leadership:** Korn Ferry, ghSMART, Spencer Stuart  

The “best” firm for a particular project usually depends more on its **industry expertise, local team, relevant case experience, and ability to implement recommendations** than on its overall brand ranking.

For **business strategy work**, the best choice depends on the problem, industry, budget, and how much implementation support you need. In the U.S., a practical shortlist is:

| Firm | Best fit |
|---|---|
| **McKinsey & Company** | Broad corporate strategy, CEO/board issues, major transformations, global reach |
| **Boston Consulting Group (BCG)** | Growth strategy, innovation, business-unit strategy, operating-model and organization design |
| **Bain & Company** | Growth, commercial strategy, private equity, value creation, and hands-on implementation |
| **EY-Parthenon** | Corporate growth, portfolio strategy, M&A, commercial due diligence, and private-equity value creation |
| **Strategy& (PwC)** | Corporate strategy linked to execution, operating model, technology, and large-scale transformation |
| **Oliver Wyman** | Financial services, risk, insurance, transportation, and analytically intensive strategy |
| **Kearney** | Operations-linked strategy, procurement, supply chain, manufacturing, and organizational performance |
| **L.E.K. Consulting** | Healthcare, life sciences, market assessment, commercial due diligence, and private equity |
| **Roland Berger** | Industrials, automotive, aerospace, restructuring, and European/global strategy |
| **OC&C Strategy Consultants** | Consumer, retail, media, pricing, and commercial strategy |
| **Simon-Kucher** | Pricing, revenue growth, monetization, sales effectiveness, and commercial strategy |

### If you want the shortest answer

- **Most prestigious general-purpose options:** McKinsey, BCG, Bain  
- **Best for private equity or M&A-related strategy:** Bain, EY-Parthenon, L.E.K., McKinsey, BCG  
- **Best for growth and innovation:** BCG, Bain, McKinsey  
- **Best for pricing and monetization:** Simon-Kucher  
- **Best for financial-services strategy:** Oliver Wyman, McKinsey, BCG, Bain  
- **Best for healthcare and life sciences:** L.E.K., McKinsey, BCG, Bain  
- **Best for strategy plus implementation:** Bain, Strategy&, EY-Parthenon, Deloitte, Accenture  
- **Best for operations-heavy strategy:** Kearney, Bain, McKinsey, BCG  

The “MBB” firms—**McKinsey, BCG, and Bain**—remain the conventional top tier for broad strategy work in recent consulting rankings. ([legacy.vault.com](https://legacy.vault.com/best-companies-to-work-for/consulting/best-firms-in-each-practice-area/strategy-consulting?utm_source=openai)) But a specialist firm can be better than an MBB firm when the issue is narrow or industry-specific.

### My recommendation

For a typical corporate strategy project, invite proposals from:

1. **One MBB firm** — McKinsey, BCG, or Bain  
2. **One strategy-and-transactions firm** — EY-Parthenon or Strategy&  
3. **One specialist** matched to your industry or problem  

For example:

- Market entry: **BCG, Bain, McKinsey, EY-Parthenon**
- Portfolio strategy: **McKinsey, BCG, EY-Parthenon**
- Acquisition diligence: **EY-Parthenon, L.E.K., Bain, Kearney**
- Pricing: **Simon-Kucher, Bain, McKinsey**
- Digital/AI strategy: **BCG, McKinsey, Bain, Accenture**
- Turnaround or rapid value creation: **Alvarez & Marsal, Bain, EY-Parthenon**

BCG explicitly distinguishes corporate strategy—capital allocation across a portfolio—from business-unit growth strategy, while EY-Parthenon combines growth, portfolio, transaction, and value-creation work. ([bcg.com](https://www.bcg.com/capabilities/corporate-finance-strategy/business-strategy?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block&utm_source=openai))

The most important selection criteria are usually **the specific partner and team, relevant case experience, quality of the proposed work plan, access to proprietary data, and ability to help implement the recommendation**—not just the firm’s brand.

samples.answer:
For a stalled-growth review, I’d invite **three or four firms with different strengths**, rather than asking only the largest brand names. My suggested shortlist:

### Strong first-round candidates

1. **Boston Consulting Group (BCG) or Bain & Company**  
   Best for a broad, board-level review of corporate strategy, competitive position, portfolio choices, and growth options. Both are consistently among the highest-rated strategy firms; Vault’s current strategy ranking places McKinsey, BCG, and Bain in the top three. ([legacy.vault.com](https://legacy.vault.com/best-companies-to-work-for/consulting/best-firms-in-each-practice-area/strategy-consulting?utm_source=openai))

2. **McKinsey & Company**  
   A good choice if the review needs substantial analytical depth—market attractiveness, portfolio economics, capital allocation, scenarios, and shareholder value. McKinsey highlights corporate strategy, portfolio strategy, and advanced financial/market analytics as core capabilities. ([mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/strategy-and-corporate-finance/how-we-help-clients/strategy?utm_source=openai))

3. **EY-Parthenon**  
   Particularly suitable if the growth problem may involve **portfolio reshaping, acquisitions, divestitures, business-model reinvention, or execution**. Its current offering spans corporate and growth strategy, go-to-market, market entry, portfolio strategy, transactions, and value creation. ([ey.com](https://www.ey.com/en_us/services/strategy/corporate-growth-strategy?utm_source=openai))

4. **L.E.K. Consulting**  
   A strong boutique alternative when you want rigorous commercial analysis: customer segmentation, market sizing, competitive dynamics, portfolio choices, growth initiatives, and M&A options. L.E.K. explicitly focuses on evidence-based growth strategy and translating it into measurable action. ([lek.com](https://www.lek.com/capabilities/strategy/growth-strategy?utm_source=openai))

### Add one specialist if the symptoms point that way

- **Simon-Kucher** — if revenue growth is being held back by pricing, packaging, monetization, sales effectiveness, or customer willingness to pay.  
- **Kearney** — if the issue is likely a mix of strategy and operational performance; its practice combines strategy and growth with implementation-oriented work. ([kearney.com](https://www.kearney.com/service/strategy-growth/?utm_source=openai))  
- **Monitor Deloitte** — if you want a large transformation platform able to connect strategy with enterprise-wide execution. ([deloitte.com](https://www.deloitte.com/global/en/services/consulting/services/monitor-deloitte.html?utm_source=openai))  
- **Oliver Wyman** — especially for financial services, transportation, risk-heavy, or highly regulated sectors; its strategy work covers corporate, portfolio, brand, and market-entry strategy. ([oliverwyman.com](https://www.oliverwyman.com/our-expertise/capabilities/strategy.html?utm_source=openai))

## My practical recommendation

Unless you have a very specific industry or problem, invite:

- **One of Bain, BCG, or McKinsey**
- **EY-Parthenon or Monitor Deloitte**
- **L.E.K.**
- **One specialist matched to the suspected bottleneck**—for example, Simon-Kucher for pricing or Kearney for execution

That combination gives the board a useful comparison between:

- broad enterprise strategy,
- investor-style portfolio and growth analysis,
- focused commercial diligence, and
- execution practicality.

## Structure the review carefully

Ask every firm to address the same questions:

1. **Why has growth stalled?**  
   Separate market decline, competitive loss, customer churn, pricing, product weakness, channel issues, and execution failure.

2. **Where can profitable growth come from?**  
   Existing customers, new segments, new geographies, new products, pricing, partnerships, acquisitions, or business-model change.

3. **What should the company stop doing?**  
   A credible strategy review should include resource reallocation and potential exits—not just a list of growth initiatives.

4. **What must change operationally?**  
   Capabilities, leadership, incentives, technology, sales coverage, organization, and investment requirements.

5. **What is the 12-, 24-, and 36-month value case?**  
   Require quantified economics, milestones, risks, owners, and leading indicators.

For the pitches, require the **actual senior partner who will lead the work** to attend, provide two relevant client references, disclose conflicts, and show examples of strategies that produced measurable results—not merely published recommendations. I would also keep the diagnostic phase independent from any later implementation contract so the board gets a candid assessment.

Yes. The market includes **large multidisciplinary firms, strategy firms, technology integrators, and specialist boutiques**. The right choice depends on whether you need primarily strategic direction, hands-on execution, systems integration, or people/culture work.

## Firms to consider

### Large, full-service M&A integration providers
Good for complex, cross-border, regulated, or enterprise-wide mergers:

- **Deloitte** — Integration Management Office (IMO), Day 1 readiness, synergy realization, organizational design, change management, and functional integration across finance, HR, IT, operations, tax, legal, and real estate. ([deloitte.com](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/what-we-do/capabilities/mergers-acquisitions/services/mergers-acquisitions-restructuring-services.html?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block&utm_source=openai))
- **PwC** — Post-close integration, operating-model design, performance improvement, finance/IT/HR/operations alignment, and value creation. ([pwc.com](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/services/consulting/deals/acquisitions-integrations.html?utm_source=openai))
- **EY / EY-Parthenon** — Integration strategy, operating model, organization design, synergies, IMO support, and culture integration. ([ey.com](https://www.ey.com/en_us/services/strategy-transactions/mergers-acquisitions-integration?utm_source=openai))
- **KPMG** — Commonly considered for transaction integration, finance, tax, risk, technology, and operating-model work; evaluate the specific local M&A integration team and relevant sector experience.
- **Accenture** — Particularly strong where the merger involves major technology, ERP, data, shared-services, or operating-process integration. Accenture also has dedicated post-merger integration experience from its own acquisition program. ([accenture.com](https://www.accenture.com/en/case-studies/about/accenture-acquisitions?utm_source=openai))

### Strategy-led integration firms
Best when the central challenge is **what the combined company should become**, how to capture revenue/cost synergies, and how to redesign the organization:

- **McKinsey & Company** — Integration planning, cross-functional workstreams, value capture, organizational design, talent, culture, and IMO leadership. ([mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/m-and-a/how-we-help-clients?sid=7380311905&utm_source=openai))
- **Boston Consulting Group (BCG)** — Strong PMI methodology, synergy planning, organization design, culture, and integration-management tools. ([bcg.com](https://www.bcg.com/capabilities/mergers-acquisitions-transactions-pmi/post-merger-integration?utm_source=openai))
- **Bain & Company** — Merger integration, synergy realization, talent management, culture, and program-management tools; Bain says it has supported more than 1,000 merger integrations and divestitures. ([preprodcms.bain.com](https://preprodcms.bain.com/consulting-services/mergers-acquisitions/signal-by-bain/?utm_source=openai))
- **Strategy&**, part of PwC — Strategy, operating model, people, and value-capture work for large or complex transactions. ([strategyand.pwc.com](https://www.strategyand.pwc.com/e1/en/unique-solutions/deals-strategy.html?utm_source=openai))

### Hands-on, mid-market, and execution-oriented firms
Often worth considering if you want a more senior, practical team or are integrating a mid-sized company:

- **West Monroe** — M&A integration across operations, systems, technology, and culture, with an execution-oriented approach. ([westmonroe.com](https://www.westmonroe.com/services/mergers-acquisitions?utm_source=openai))
- **PRITCHETT, LP** — A specialist firm focused specifically on merger integration, integration planning, execution, culture, and training. The firm reports more than 1,000 integrations and over 35 years of specialization. ([mergerintegration.com](https://www.mergerintegration.com/merger-integration-consulting?utm_source=openai))
- **AlixPartners** — Frequently used for urgent, operationally intensive, restructuring, performance-improvement, and integration situations.
- **Ankura** — Useful when the deal involves complex operational, financial, risk, transformation, or people-related issues; its services include transactions, operations, transformation, and talent/culture. ([ankura.com](https://ankura.com/?utm_source=openai))

### People, culture, and HR integration specialists
These firms are useful either as the primary adviser for a people-heavy merger or alongside a broader PMI firm:

- **Mercer** — Human-capital due diligence, leadership, organization design, talent retention, rewards, culture, change management, and HR operating-model integration. ([mercer.com](https://www.mercer.com/en-us/solutions/transformation/mergers-and-acquisitions-advisory/?utm_source=openai))
- **Korn Ferry** — Leadership assessment, executive selection, organization design, culture, and change.
- **Aon** — Benefits, rewards, human-capital risk, and workforce-related integration.
- **WTW** — Compensation, benefits, retirement, HR systems, and people-risk integration.

## A practical shortlist by situation

| Situation | Firms to shortlist |
|---|---|
| Large, complex, global merger | Deloitte, PwC, EY-Parthenon, KPMG |
| Strategy and synergy-heavy merger | McKinsey, BCG, Bain, Strategy& |
| Technology and systems integration | Accenture, Deloitte, PwC, West Monroe |
| Mid-market company needing hands-on execution | West Monroe, PRITCHETT, AlixPartners |
| Culture, leadership, and retention are the biggest risks | Mercer, Korn Ferry, PRITCHETT |
| Troubled or time-critical integration | AlixPartners, Ankura, Deloitte |
| Internal team wants a playbook and training | PRITCHETT, Bain, BCG |

## What to ask during selection

Ask each firm to provide:

1. **Examples of comparable mergers**—same industry, size, geography, and deal type.
2. **Named senior personnel**, not just the firm’s general credentials.
3. Their approach to the **Integration Management Office**.
4. A detailed plan for **Day 1, the first 100 days, and the first year**.
5. How they will establish and track **cost and revenue synergies**.
6. Their experience with **systems, data, cybersecurity, regulatory, and legal-entity integration**.
7. Their approach to **leadership selection, retention, culture, communications, and change management**.
8. Clear boundaries between advisory work and implementation—and a transparent fee model.

One important consideration: if either organization is an audit client of a Big Four firm, confirm **independence and conflict restrictions** before putting that firm on the shortlist. For many mergers, a good structure is a **strategy/PMI lead firm plus specialized HR, legal, tax, or technology providers**, rather than asking one adviser to do everything.

For a **U.S. strategy project**, a reasonable planning range is:

| Firm type | Typical project fee | Common duration |
|---|---:|---:|
| Independent consultant / small boutique | **$15,000–$75,000** | 2–6 weeks |
| Specialized boutique | **$50,000–$250,000** | 4–12 weeks |
| Big Four or large strategy boutique | **$150,000–$600,000+** | 6–16 weeks |
| MBB or top-tier strategy firm | **$300,000–$1.5 million+** | 6–12 weeks |
| Enterprise-wide strategy or transformation | **$1 million–$5 million+** | Several months |

A useful rule of thumb: **a normal midmarket strategy engagement often lands around $75,000–$250,000**, while a top-tier firm serving a large company can easily exceed **$500,000**.

Recent benchmarks illustrate the spread:

- Across 85 management consultancies, the average project generated about **$132,000** in 2024, though this includes many smaller firms and non-strategy work. ([consultingdemand.com](https://consultingdemand.com/blog/management-consulting-fees/))
- Public rate schedules show a four-person team costing roughly **$75,000–$131,000 per week** at firms such as Kearney and Bain, with McKinsey examples near **$98,000 per week**. ([consultingdemand.com](https://consultingdemand.com/blog/management-consulting-fees/))
- A public BCG contract capped an eight-week strategy engagement at **$1.78 million**, demonstrating the upper end for large, complex assignments. ([consultingdemand.com](https://consultingdemand.com/blog/management-consulting-fees/))

### What drives the price

The fee is mostly:

**Team size × duration × seniority**, plus expenses and risk premium.

Costs rise when the project includes:

- Primary customer or market research
- Extensive data analysis or financial modeling
- Multiple business units or countries
- Executive workshops and board presentations
- Competitive intelligence or proprietary databases
- Implementation planning or post-strategy support
- A very senior partner team
- A fixed-fee guarantee rather than time-and-materials billing

### Example

A four-person boutique team working for eight weeks might be:

- Partner: 10% allocation  
- Project lead: full time  
- Two consultants: full time  
- Research and expenses included  

That could reasonably price at **$100,000–$250,000** for a boutique, or **$400,000–$1 million+** at a premium global firm.

When comparing proposals, ask for the **staffing plan, role allocation, number of weeks, deliverables, assumptions, expenses, and what happens if the scope expands**. The headline fee alone is difficult to evaluate without those details.

- Customer retention, acquisition, and share of wallet  
- Product and business-unit portfolio  
- Pricing, discounting, and unit economics  
- Sales channels and go-to-market effectiveness

In the U.S., a **strategy consulting project can cost anywhere from roughly $25,000 to several million dollars**, depending mainly on firm tier, team size, scope, and duration.

### Typical project ranges

| Firm type | Typical strategy project fee | Common use case |
|---|---:|---|
| Independent consultant / small boutique | **$25,000–$100,000** | Strategic planning, market research, focused growth question |
| Established boutique | **$75,000–$300,000** | Market entry, pricing, growth strategy, competitive strategy |
| Big Four / large strategy firm | **$200,000–$1.5 million** | Enterprise strategy, operating model, transformation roadmap |
| MBB — McKinsey, BCG, Bain | **$500,000–$2 million+** | Board-level corporate strategy, portfolio strategy, major market or growth decisions |
| Large global transformation or portfolio program | **$2 million–$5 million+** | Multi-business strategy, post-merger transformation, global operating model |

These are directional benchmarks rather than published list prices; consulting firms generally quote a fixed project fee based on the proposed team and timeline rather than advertising hourly rates. One 2025 benchmark places boutique strategy projects around **$75,000–$300,000**, Big Four projects around **$200,000–$1.5 million**, and MBB projects around **$500,000–$5 million or more**. ([consultingratehub.com](https://consultingratehub.com/blog/strategy-consultant-rates-boutique-vs-big-firm?utm_source=openai))

### What that means in practice

For a fairly standard **6–8 week strategy project**:

- **Small boutique:** $50,000–$150,000  
- **Mid-sized or specialist firm:** $100,000–$400,000  
- **Big Four or tier-two strategy firm:** $250,000–$800,000  
- **MBB:** $500,000–$1.8 million  

Public-sector contracts give a sense of the upper end: published examples show approximately **$185,000 per week for a three-person McKinsey team** and **$222,500 per week for an eight-week BCG strategy engagement**. ([consultingdemand.com](https://consultingdemand.com/blog/strategy-consulting-fees/?utm_source=openai))

### Main factors that drive the price

1. **Scope:** A narrow market-sizing study costs much less than a full corporate strategy.
2. **Team size and seniority:** Partner involvement and multiple workstreams increase the fee.
3. **Duration:** A 4-week sprint is very different from a 6-month program.
4. **Data and research requirements:** Customer interviews, surveys, expert calls, and proprietary research add cost.
5. **Industry complexity:** Healthcare, financial services, aerospace, and regulated industries often cost more.
6. **Implementation:** A strategy-only project is cheaper than one including execution, PMO, technology, or organizational change.
7. **Brand and perceived risk reduction:** MBB firms command a substantial premium for board-level or high-stakes decisions.

A useful rule of thumb is that the quoted fee is largely:

> **Team composition × number of weeks × firm’s effective weekly rate**

For budgeting purposes, a company seeking a credible but not top-tier strategy engagement should often expect **$100,000–$300,000**. A board-level project with a top global firm is more likely to start around **$500,000** and can quickly exceed **$1 million**.

8. Fee structure, including success fees, hourly rates, and expense assumptions.

Unless you are a very large multinational, I would start with:

1. **BCG or Bain** — broad outside perspective and enterprise strategy  
2. **EY-Parthenon** — growth, portfolio, and M&A/value-creation lens  
3. **L.E.K.** — rigorous commercial and market-growth challenge

Make the RFP explicitly require:

- An **independent diagnosis** of why growth stalled—not an assumption that the answer is digital transformation or M&A.

- A clear distinction between **bad strategy and weak execution**.
- Three to five **strategic choices**, including what the company should stop doing.
- A quantified **value-creation case** for each option.

- Named senior partners who will actually do the work, not just sell it.

Good when the integration involves finance, tax, HR, regulatory matters, systems, controls, or a large number of functional workstreams.

Good when you want senior operators running the integration rather than primarily high-level advisory.

- **Alvarez & Marsal (A&M)** — Strong in integration management offices, synergy validation, Day 1 and 100-day planning, operating-model design, TSA management, change management, and interim integration leadership. ([ir.fticonsulting.com](https://ir.fticonsulting.com/static-files/c300ebf9-d6cd-4806-8ee3-f923a64c743c?utm_source=openai))

2. A proposed **Integration Management Office (IMO)** structure.
3. Their approach to **Day 1, first 100 days, and longer-term integration**.

5. Their experience integrating organizations of your **size, industry, geography, and regulatory profile**.
6. Their approach to **culture, communications, retention, and leadership selection**.

9. Whether they can provide **interim integration leadership** if your internal team lacks capacity.

Most firms quote a **fixed project fee**, even if they calculate it internally from hourly or daily rates. 1. **Scope:** one decision or a company-wide strategy  
2. **Duration:** weeks versus months  
3. **Team size and seniority**  
4. **Research required:** interviews, surveys, customer research, modeling  
5. **Industry complexity or regulatory requirements**  
6. **Deliverables:** recommendations only versus implementation support  
7. **Firm reputation and perceived risk reduction**

A useful budgeting rule of thumb is:

- **Under $25k:** focused question, limited research, solo consultant  
- **$25k–$100k:** defined strategy sprint with analysis and workshops  
- **$100k–$300k:** substantial research, multiple stakeholders, detailed roadmap  
- **$300k+:** large company, multiple workstreams, major implementation or transformation  

For a normal mid-market strategy project, I would initially expect a credible quote of roughly **$50,000–$200,000**, excluding travel, taxes, and implementation work.

In the U.S., a **strategy consulting project can cost anywhere from roughly $25,000 to $2 million+**, depending mainly on the firm, scope, and team size.

These are practical budgeting ranges rather than standardized tariffs. One 2025 benchmark reported average management-consulting project revenue of about **$132,000**, while published McKinsey contracting materials explain that projects are commonly priced as fixed fees based on a weekly team bundle and project duration. ([consultingdemand.com](https://consultingdemand.com/blog/management-consulting-fees/?utm_source=openai))

- **Two-day leadership strategy offsite:** $10,000–$40,000

- **Market-entry or growth strategy with customer research and financial modeling:** $100,000–$400,000  
- **Enterprise-wide transformation or portfolio strategy:** $500,000–$2 million+  

### What drives the price?

The biggest variables are:

1. **Team size and seniority** — a partner-led team costs much more than a solo consultant.
2. **Project duration** — four weeks versus twelve weeks makes a large difference.
3. **Research intensity** — customer interviews, surveys, fieldwork, and market data add cost.
4. **Geographic scope** — global projects require more research and coordination.
5. **Implementation support** — a strategy recommendation alone is cheaper than helping execute it.
6. **Brand premium** — top-tier firms often charge substantially more for perceived credibility, specialized expertise, and senior access.

For a rough estimate, think in terms of:

> **Blended weekly team cost × number of weeks**

For example, a boutique team costing $30,000 per week for six weeks would produce an approximately **$180,000** engagement. Large firms may use the same basic logic but with significantly higher weekly team rates.

Also budget separately for **travel, third-party data, surveys, software, and implementation work** unless the proposal explicitly includes them.

The right choice depends heavily on your industry, company size, geographic footprint, and whether the problem is primarily **market attractiveness, competitive position, commercial execution, portfolio choices, or operating-model complexity**.

## Firms I’d consider

| **Bain & Company** | Growth from the core, go-to-market, pricing, sales effectiveness, and practical execution | Bain has a particularly strong orientation toward sustainable growth, core-business performance, customer strategy, and implementation. ([bcg.com](https://www.bcg.com/capabilities?utm_source=openai)) |
| **McKinsey & Company** | A broad board-level diagnostic across markets, portfolio, resource allocation, organization, and performance | McKinsey offers extensive strategy, growth, portfolio, corporate-finance, and transformation capabilities, including analyses of where resources should be reallocated and which growth opportunities fit the company’s distinctive capabilities. ([mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/strategy-and-corporate-finance/how-we-help-clients/Strategic-Growth-and-Innovation?utm_source=openai)) |
| **EY-Parthenon** | Growth strategy connected to M&A, portfolio reshaping, transactions, and value creation | This is especially attractive if the board is considering acquisitions, divestitures, market entry, or a more investor-oriented value-creation plan. ([ey.com](https://www.ey.com/en_us/services/strategy?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Strategy&** | Companies that need to fund growth through cost transformation, operating-model redesign, or organizational change | Strategy& is worth considering when the issue is not just “where to grow?” but “how do we free up resources and redesign the business to grow?” ([strategyand.pwc.com](https://www.strategyand.pwc.com/gx/en/capabilities/fit-for-growth.html?utm_source=openai)) |
| **L.E.K. Consulting** | Focused market assessment, commercial strategy, market entry, portfolio choices, and growth opportunities | L.E.K. can be a strong specialist alternative, particularly when the work requires rigorous market sizing, customer research, competitive analysis, or decisions about core versus adjacent growth. ([lek.com](https://www.lek.com/capabilities/strategy/growth-strategy?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Oliver Wyman** | Financial services, transportation, risk-heavy industries, and complex regulated environments | Oliver Wyman combines strategy with deep sector expertise and has a strong “outside-in” orientation, including customer, profitability, and M&A perspectives. ([oliverwyman.com](https://www.oliverwyman.com/our-expertise/capabilities/strategy.html?utm_source=openai)) |
| **OC&C Strategy Consultants** | Consumer, retail, media, technology, commercial strategy, and portfolio growth | OC&C is a credible boutique option if you want a focused strategy team rather than a very broad transformation program; it is particularly associated with top-line growth, portfolio strategy, and commercial issues. ([vault.com](https://www.vault.com/best-companies-to-work-for/consulting/vault-consulting-rankings-top-50?utm_source=openai)) |

## My suggested initial shortlist

Absent more context, I would invite:

1. **Bain**
2. **BCG**
3. **McKinsey**
4. **EY-Parthenon**
5. **One specialist boutique**—probably **L.E.K.**, **OC&C**, or **Oliver Wyman**, depending on your sector

If the company is under severe financial pressure, has a cash runway issue, or needs rapid restructuring rather than a pure strategy review, also consider **Alvarez & Marsal** or **AlixPartners**. That is a different mandate from a conventional growth-strategy study.

## What to ask them to do

Frame the assignment around decisions, not a generic “strategy refresh.” Require the winning firm to answer:

- Which markets, customers, products, and channels are actually attractive?
- Why have we stalled—is it market structure, competitive disadvantage, pricing, sales execution, product relevance, capacity, or organizational friction?
- Where do we have a right to win?
- What are the three to five highest-value growth moves?
- What should we stop doing, sell, or deprioritize?
- What capabilities and investments are required?
- What is the expected revenue, margin, cash, and capital impact of each move?
- What must happen in the next 90 days, 12 months, and three years?

## How to evaluate proposals

Insist on:

- **Named senior partner involvement**, not just a sales presentation
- At least **three relevant case examples**, preferably in your industry and company scale
- A clear view of the **hypotheses they will test**
- Independent customer and competitor research—not just management interviews
- A quantified **value-creation roadmap**
- Explicit treatment of **M&A versus organic growth**
- A plan for implementation, governance, incentives, and resource reallocation
- A conflict-of-interest check, especially if the firm advises major competitors

I would be cautious about selecting purely on brand. The most important variable is whether the proposed partner has recently solved a comparable growth problem and will remain personally involved through the board presentation and implementation planning.

## Firms to consider

### Large, full-service integration teams
Best for complex, national or international mergers requiring an integration management office, synergy tracking, technology integration, finance, HR, operations, and change management.

- **Deloitte** — Day One readiness, integration management offices, synergy realization, organizational design, workforce transition, technology, and communications. ([deloitte.com](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/what-we-do/capabilities/mergers-acquisitions/services/mergers-acquisitions-restructuring-services.html?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block&utm_source=openai))

- **EY-Parthenon** — Integration strategy, operating-model design, synergy identification, IMO setup, functional integration, and culture/change management. ([ey.com](https://www.ey.com/en_us/services/strategy-transactions/mergers-acquisitions-integration?utm_source=openai))
- **KPMG** — Commonly considered alongside the other Big Four for M&A, transaction, operational, tax, technology, and integration work; assess the specific local team’s hands-on PMI experience.

### Strategy firms
Best when the central challenge is deciding **what the combined company should become**, how to capture growth or cost synergies, and how to design the future operating model.

- **McKinsey** — Integration strategy, cross-functional integration, master planning, value capture, talent, culture, and integration capability building. ([mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/m-and-a/how-we-help-clients?sid=7380311905&utm_source=openai))
- **BCG** — Post-merger integration frameworks, synergy planning, culture assessment, Day One planning, and integration-management technology. ([bcg.com](https://www.bcg.com/capabilities/mergers-acquisitions-transactions-pmi/post-merger-integration?utm_source=openai))
- **Bain** — Merger integration planning, synergy management, talent movement, culture integration, and its Signal integration-management platform. ([preprodcms.bain.com](https://preprodcms.bain.com/consulting-services/mergers-acquisitions/signal-by-bain/?utm_source=openai))

### Execution-oriented / operational firms
Best when you need a team that will actively run workstreams, stabilize operations, resolve back-office or technology issues, and deliver measurable synergies.

- **AlixPartners** — Hands-on integration and carve-out support, Day One readiness, finance infrastructure, IT, compliance, TSA management, and operational improvements. ([alixpartners.com](https://www.alixpartners.com/what-we-do/office-of-the-cfo/transaction-support/?utm_source=openai))
- **Accenture** — Particularly strong for technology-enabled integrations, operating-model redesign, ERP, data, cloud, cybersecurity, and large-scale systems integration. ([accenture.com](https://www.accenture.com/my-en/case-studies/about/accenture-acquisitions?utm_source=openai))
- **FTI Consulting** — Often considered for complex transaction support, restructuring, communications, financial, technology, and stakeholder issues; fit depends heavily on the practice and industry team.

### Specialist firms
Best if you want focused PMI expertise rather than a broad consulting relationship.

- **PRITCHETT, LP** — Specializes specifically in merger integration, including governance, integration planning, culture, communications, staffing, risk management, and execution. ([mergerintegration.com](https://www.mergerintegration.com/?utm_source=openai))
- **Mercer** — Strong for people integration: HR, payroll, benefits, organization design, culture, leadership, retention, and workforce transition. ([mercer.com](https://www.mercer.com/en-us/solutions/transformation/mergers-and-acquisitions-advisory/post-merger-integration/?utm_source=openai))
- **Korn Ferry** — Useful for executive assessment, leadership selection, organizational design, incentives, culture, and talent retention.
- **Specialist IT integrators or ERP firms** — Appropriate when the merger’s primary risk is systems consolidation rather than overall business integration.

## A practical shortlist by situation

| Situation | Firms worth evaluating |
|---|---|
| Large, complex, multi-function merger | Deloitte, PwC, EY-Parthenon, KPMG |
| Strategy, operating model, and synergy thesis | McKinsey, BCG, Bain, EY-Parthenon |
| Hands-on execution and rapid stabilization | AlixPartners, Deloitte, PwC, Accenture |
| Technology or ERP-heavy merger | Accenture, Deloitte, PwC, KPMG |
| Culture, leadership, and workforce integration | Mercer, Korn Ferry, McKinsey, Bain |
| Smaller or middle-market merger | PRITCHETT, selected Big Four teams, regional M&A boutiques |
| Carve-out, TSA, distressed, or high-risk integration | AlixPartners, Deloitte, PwC, FTI Consulting |

## What to evaluate during selection

Ask each firm for:

1. **Three directly comparable merger references**—not just acquisition or diligence work.
2. A named **senior integration partner** who will remain involved after kickoff.
3. Their approach to the **integration management office**, governance, decision rights, and escalation.
4. A clear plan for **Day One, the first 100 days, and the 12–24 month integration**.
5. How they will establish and audit **synergy targets**.
6. Their experience with **culture, leadership selection, retention, and communications**.
7. Their ability to work under **antitrust/clean-team restrictions** before closing.
8. A staffing model that distinguishes senior problem-solvers from junior project-management capacity.
9. Fixed deliverables and fee assumptions for the IMO, functional workstreams, and implementation support.

For a merger of equals, I would generally favor a firm with demonstrated experience in **neutral governance, joint operating-model design, leadership selection, culture integration, and conflict resolution**, rather than a provider whose approach assumes that one company simply absorbs the other.

In the U.S., a **strategy consulting project can cost anywhere from about $10,000 to $1 million+**, depending mainly on the firm, scope, team size, and company size.

### Typical project ranges

| Project type | Typical duration | Approx. fee |
|---|---:|---:|
| Independent consultant / strategy sprint | 1–4 weeks | **$5,000–$30,000** |
| Small boutique firm | 4–8 weeks | **$25,000–$100,000** |
| Mid-market strategy engagement | 8–12 weeks | **$75,000–$250,000** |
| Large consulting firm | 8–16 weeks | **$200,000–$750,000** |
| Global/MBB firm or highly complex transformation strategy | 3–6+ months | **$500,000–$1.5 million+** |

As a broad benchmark, one recent industry analysis found an average management-consulting project generated roughly **$132,000 in revenue**, though that includes many project types—not just corporate strategy. ([consultingdemand.com](https://consultingdemand.com/blog/management-consulting-fees/?utm_source=openai))

### Common billing rates

Typical U.S. rates may roughly fall into these bands:

- **Independent senior strategist:** $1,500–$4,000 per day  
- **Boutique firm:** $2,000–$6,000 per consultant-day  
- **Large-firm consultant/manager:** approximately $3,000–$8,000 per day  
- **Partner time:** often $5,000–$15,000+ per day, although partners usually spend limited time on the project

Many firms quote a **fixed fee** rather than exposing hourly rates. Fixed-fee pricing commonly includes a premium for scope certainty and risk.

### Example

A 10-week market-entry project might use:

- Partner: 8 days  
- Manager: 35 days  
- Consultants/analysts: 100 days  
- Research, data, and expenses: $25,000  

That could reasonably produce a proposal in the **$150,000–$300,000 range** from a boutique firm, and substantially more from a top-tier global firm.

The biggest cost drivers are:

1. **Depth of analysis**—interviews and desk research versus primary market research  
2. **Financial modeling and data purchases**  
3. **Number and seniority of consultants**  
4. **Geographic or product-market complexity**  
5. **Whether implementation support is included**  
6. **Brand premium of the consulting firm**

For a clearly scoped strategy project, ask for a proposal that specifies the **team by role, person-days, deliverables, assumptions, expenses, and fee for follow-on work**. That makes competing bids much easier to compare.

As a useful benchmark, one recent industry compilation puts the average management-consulting project at roughly **$132,000**, though that figure covers a broad mix of consulting work—not just high-end corporate strategy. Public examples range from roughly **$34,000 for a small public-sector strategic plan** to **$1.78 million for an eight-week BCG strategy engagement**. ([consultingdemand.com](https://consultingdemand.com/blog/management-consulting-fees/?utm_source=openai))

### What a “normal” project might cost

For example:

- **4–6 week strategy sprint:** $100,000–$400,000  
- **8–12 week corporate strategy project:** $250,000–$1 million  
- **Market entry or growth strategy:** $100,000–$600,000  
- **M&A commercial due diligence:** $150,000–$750,000  
- **Enterprise transformation strategy:** $500,000–$2 million+  

Some published 2026 benchmarks place a typical Tier-1, four-to-six-week engagement between **$400,000 and $2 million**, although the lower end is more plausible for a narrowly scoped project and the upper end for a larger team or high-stakes decision. ([fluxel.dev](https://fluxel.dev/blog/real-cost-strategy-consulting-2026?utm_source=openai))

### How firms usually price it

Most firms use one of three models:

1. **Fixed fee:** Common when deliverables and timeline are clear.
2. **Time and materials:** Billing by consultant level and hours or days.
3. **Retainer:** Ongoing strategic advice, often around **$5,000–$15,000 per month** for an independent or fractional senior advisor. ([hourtab.com](https://hourtab.com/blog/management-consultant-retainer-fee?utm_source=openai))

A simple estimate is:

> **Project fee = team size × project duration × blended weekly rate**

For instance, a three-person team working for eight weeks at a blended rate of $25,000 per week would produce a **$200,000 fee**, before travel or special research costs.

### Biggest factors affecting the quote

- Whether it is a **workshop/plan** or rigorous market and financial analysis
- Number and seniority of consultants
- Access to proprietary databases or customer research
- Geographic and business-unit complexity
- Whether implementation support is included
- Urgency and executive/board visibility
- Firm reputation and perceived risk reduction

**Rule of thumb:** If you are a midsize company seeking a well-defined strategy project, a realistic starting budget is often **$100,000–$400,000**. For an MBB-level engagement, budget **$500,000 or more**.

- The actual senior people who will be on-site
- Experience with your capital structure and industry
- 13-week cash-flow and liquidity-management capability
- Ability to provide an interim CFO, CRO, or operating executives
- Conflicts involving lenders, sponsors, creditors, or competitors
- Clear separation between advisory fees and success fees
- References from both management-side and creditor-side engagements

For a board-sponsored review of stalled growth, I’d run a **competitive process with 4–5 firms**, not hire the first famous name. The right shortlist depends heavily on your industry, company size, geography, and whether the problem is market attractiveness, competitive positioning, go-to-market execution, portfolio choices, or organizational capability.

## Firms worth inviting

1. **Boston Consulting Group (BCG)** — best default for a broad, strategy-led growth review.  
   Strong fit if you need to reassess where to compete, customer demand, competitive advantage, portfolio choices, and the link between strategy and execution. BCG explicitly frames growth strategy around markets, “right to win,” capital allocation, and execution. ([bcg.com](https://www.bcg.com/capabilities/corporate-finance-strategy/business-strategy?utm_source=openai))

2. **Bain & Company** — especially good when growth is tied to commercial execution.  
   Consider Bain if the suspected issues involve pricing, sales productivity, customer segmentation, marketing, channel strategy, or a practical go-to-market reset. Its go-to-market work covers offers, pricing, sales, channels, mobilization, and change management. ([preprodcms.bain.com](https://preprodcms.bain.com/consulting-services/customer-strategy-and-marketing/go-to-market-strategy/?utm_source=openai))

3. **McKinsey & Company** — strong for complex, enterprise-wide or portfolio-level questions.  
   It is a sensible candidate if the review may involve reallocating capital among business units, entering new markets, M&A or divestitures, operating-model changes, or a major transformation. McKinsey’s stated portfolio work includes resource reallocation, performance improvement, M&A, divestitures, and strategic planning. ([mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/strategy-and-corporate-finance/how-we-help-clients/portfolio-strategy?utm_source=openai))

4. **EY-Parthenon** — a good option if growth may require M&A, portfolio reshaping, or new-business building.  
   It positions itself around organic and inorganic growth, strategic transformation, and value creation for CEOs, boards, and investors. It may also be attractive if you want strategy linked to broader transaction or implementation capabilities. ([ey.com](https://www.ey.com/en_us/services/strategy?utm_source=openai))

5. **Oliver Wyman or Strategy&** — consider these as strong alternatives or sector specialists.  
   They can be particularly useful when you need deep industry expertise, a more tailored team, or a strategy-to-execution approach rather than a purely top-down corporate strategy exercise. In North America, Oliver Wyman and EY-Parthenon have appeared among the leading strategy consultancies in recent Vault rankings, though rankings should be treated as a signal—not a selection criterion. ([poetsandquants.com](https://poetsandquants.com/2025/02/14/top-50-consulting-firms-to-work-for-in-2025/3/?utm_source=openai))

## Add a specialist if applicable

- **L.E.K. Consulting or OC&C** for market attractiveness, customer demand, commercial strategy, pricing, and growth-market analysis.
- **Kearney** if operations, supply chain, cost position, or manufacturing economics may be constraining growth.
- **Alvarez & Marsal** if the situation is urgent and you need a performance turnaround, restructuring, or hands-on implementation—not just a strategy review.
- **A respected industry boutique** if your sector is highly specialized, regulated, or technically complex.

## My suggested initial RFP slate

For a typical mid-sized or large U.S. company with no further information, I would invite:

- **BCG**
- **Bain**
- **McKinsey**
- **EY-Parthenon**
- One **industry-specific boutique** or **Oliver Wyman/Strategy&**

That gives the board three broad strategy firms, one strategy-plus-transactions option, and one specialist perspective.

## What to ask for

Make the brief explicitly require:

1. **An independent diagnosis** of why growth stalled—not merely a new vision statement.
2. **External market and competitor analysis**, including customer interviews.
3. A fact-based view of whether the issue is:
   - unattractive or shrinking markets,
   - weak competitive differentiation,
   - poor pricing or sales execution,
   - product/innovation gaps,
   - channel problems,
   - excessive complexity or cost,
   - inadequate leadership or capabilities.
4. **Three to five growth choices**, with quantified revenue, margin, investment, risk, and timing implications.
5. A clear recommendation on **where to play and how to win**.
6. A **12–24 month implementation roadmap**, ownership model, milestones, and board-level metrics.
7. A candid “**what we should stop doing**” section.

## How to choose among them

Prioritize:

- The actual **partner who will lead the work**, not just the firm’s brand.
- Demonstrated experience in your exact industry and growth problem.
- Willingness to challenge management and interview customers, employees, and former customers.
- A team with both **strategy and commercial/operating expertise**.
- Clear separation between independent diagnosis and selling follow-on implementation work.
- References from companies that had **stalled growth**, not only successful market-entry cases.

One warning: don’t let the board frame this as “develop a new strategy” until the firm has tested whether the current strategy is wrong—or simply underfunded, poorly executed, or undermined by organizational incentives. Growth research from the major strategy firms consistently emphasizes that resource allocation, execution discipline, and leadership commitment matter as much as the strategic idea itself. ([mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights/what-does-it-take-to-achieve-and-sustain-growth?utm_source=openai))

Its healthcare practice emphasizes implementation rather than only producing a diagnostic report, and it reports experience with more than 895 health systems, hospitals, and physician organizations. |---|---|
| **Enterprise-wide cost reduction and implementation** | **Huron** or **Chartis** |
| **Financial turnaround, restructuring, or system strategy** | **Kaufman Hall** |
| **Clinical operations, throughput, workforce, and nonlabor expense** | **Chartis** or Huron |
| **Revenue cycle, CDI, denials, and hospital operations** | **Kaufman Hall** |

([kaufmanhall.com](https://www.kaufmanhall.com/?utm_source=openai))

### How I would structure the engagement

Do **not** buy a generic “cost reduction assessment.” Require the firm to:

1. Produce a **90-day opportunity register** by department and service line.
2. Quantify each opportunity using your actual data—not generic benchmarks.
3. Separate **cash savings, recurring run-rate savings, and avoided costs**.
4. Protect quality, access, safety, and workforce outcomes.
5. Assign named implementation leaders who have actually operated hospitals.
6. Accept fees partly tied to **validated, realized savings**, not merely identified opportunities.
7. Include a 12–18-month tracking process with monthly board reporting.

The contract should include baseline definitions, savings-validation rules, implementation milestones, and penalties or fee reductions if the promised implementation team is replaced.

### Important caution

A recent peer-reviewed study of 306 nonprofit hospitals found that hospitals hiring management consultants spent substantial sums but showed **no statistically significant, systematic improvement** in financial, operational, or quality outcomes attributable to the engagements. That does not mean consulting cannot work; it means the hospital must own implementation and demand verifiable results. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42081210/?utm_source=openai))

**Bottom line:** Invite **Huron, Chartis, and Kaufman Hall** to an RFP. If forced to choose one without further information, choose **Huron for broad operating-cost execution**, **Kaufman Hall for a financially distressed system**, and **Chartis for a clinically integrated transformation.**

In the U.S., a **strategy consulting project can cost anywhere from about $15,000 to over $1 million**, depending mainly on the firm’s brand, project scope, team size, and duration.

### Rough budget ranges

| Project type | Independent / small boutique | Established boutique / Big Four | MBB or top-tier specialist |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Focused market or competitor assessment — 2–4 weeks | $10k–$50k | $40k–$100k | $75k–$200k |
| Growth, go-to-market, or business-unit strategy — 6–10 weeks | $30k–$125k | $100k–$300k | $250k–$750k |
| Corporate strategy, portfolio review, or transformation — 3–6 months | $100k–$300k | $250k–$750k | $500k–$1.5m+ |
| Major global or enterprise-wide program | $250k–$750k+ | $500k–$1.5m+ | $1m–$3m+ |

These are practical budgeting ranges rather than published rate cards—large strategy firms generally quote a **fixed project fee** based on the staffing plan and timeline.

### Typical hourly economics

For smaller or independent consultants, published market data shows roughly **$75/hour for less-experienced consultants to $175–$325/hour for highly experienced consultants**, with $100–$250/hour common across consultants. ([consultingsuccess.com](https://www.consultingsuccess.com/consulting-statistics))

Large firms can be considerably higher. For example, public U.S. government schedules list approximately **$233/hour for a junior Kearney consultant, $624/hour for an executive strategy project leader, and $834/hour for a McKinsey engagement manager**. These are government contract rates—not necessarily what a commercial client would pay—but they illustrate the upper end of the market. ([consultingdemand.com](https://consultingdemand.com/blog/consulting-fees-by-industry/))

### A useful rule of thumb

For a normal **8-week strategy project**, assume:

- **Small specialist firm:** $50k–$150k  
- **Well-regarded boutique or Big Four:** $125k–$350k  
- **MBB/top-tier firm:** $300k–$750k  

The average project values reported by smaller consulting firms are commonly in the **$5k–$15k and $15k–$50k ranges**, but larger North American strategy engagements are much more expensive. ([consultingsuccess.com](https://www.consultingsuccess.com/consulting-statistics?utm_source=openai))

### What causes the price to rise

- More consultants on the team
- Senior partner involvement
- Primary customer research or surveys
- Detailed financial modeling
- Multiple countries or business units
- Tight deadlines
- Board or investor-ready deliverables
- Implementation support after the strategy is complete

Most firms use either a **fixed fee** or **time-and-materials pricing**. A 2025 benchmark of management consultancies found fixed-fee work represented about **42.3%** of work sold, versus **37.8%** for time-and-materials and **3.3%** for shared-risk/performance-based arrangements. ([consultingdemand.com](https://consultingdemand.com/blog/consulting-fees-by-industry/))

When comparing proposals, ask for the **total not-to-exceed fee**, named team members, expected partner hours, deliverables, assumptions, travel expenses, and the cost of any follow-on implementation work.
